mechanism: At-home, non-contact thermal and optical foot-imaging device with mobile app and cloud/software analysis. The FeetSee system captures plantar thermal and optical images and uses algorithmic left-right temperature asymmetry analysis to identify inflammatory hot spots that may precede diabetic foot ulceration.
development_status: ClinicalTrials.gov lists NCT07300163 as a not-yet-recruiting, prospective observational cohort study of 100 adults with diabetes, peripheral neuropathy, and recently healed plantar diabetic foot ulcer. Participants will use the FeetSee thermal camera, stand, and smartphone/tablet app at home daily for 6-9 months or until a new DFU develops; the primary objective is dataset generation and retrospective/refined algorithm testing rather than mandated treatment decisions.
expected_launch_window: Not applicable to drug pipeline launch; device/diagnostic exclusion concern
clinical_summary: FeetSee targets early identification of DFU risk through daily at-home plantar temperature monitoring. The assigned NCT07300163 study will collect longitudinal thermal/optical images in a high-risk recurrent-DFU population and estimate/refine the algorithm's sensitivity and specificity for incident DFUs, but no results are posted and the study is not yet recruiting. Prior validation research in 107 participants reported strong agreement between the FeetSee InvCam and a reference thermal camera for foot temperature measurements, with ICC 0.95 and typical error 0.31 degrees. Differentiation is supported by non-contact whole-foot imaging, app/cloud workflow, and potential accessibility for patients who cannot easily stand on a mat, but prospective outcome evidence for DFU prevention is not yet available.
safety_summary: NCT07300163 is non-interventional and states the device is used for image collection only; no experimental drug or change in standard diabetic foot care is mandated. Safety monitoring will collect and classify adverse events and device- or system-related problems. Main operational risks are delayed clinical evaluation if users over-rely on alerts, false negatives or false positives, adherence failure, technical/upload failures, privacy/security issues for images, and usability limitations in patients with cognitive, physical, vision, or mobile-device barriers.
management_tools: Exclude from drug/pharma pipeline treatment launch dashboards unless a dedicated device/diagnostic category is in scope
If covered, require high-risk diabetic foot population criteria such as diabetes, peripheral neuropathy, prior plantar DFU, and no active ulcer at initiation
Require use with ongoing standard diabetic foot care, protective footwear/offloading when indicated, and clinician follow-up for alerts or symptoms
Require FDA-approved or FDA-cleared/registered medical-device status consistent with payer policy and automatic digital data transmission where billed as RPM
Set adherence expectations for daily or near-daily image capture and continuation criteria based on usable data transmission and clinical actionability
Define provider responsibility for reviewing alerts, contacting patients, and documenting actions taken
Do not substitute device use for routine foot inspection, podiatry care, vascular assessment, wound care, or urgent evaluation of suspected ulcer/infection
evidence_gaps: No ClinicalTrials.gov results are posted for NCT07300163.
The assigned study is not yet recruiting and has estimated completion on 2027-05-30.
The study is observational and primarily intended to generate a dataset and retrospectively test/refine the algorithm, not to prove reduced DFU recurrence or amputations.
No direct FeetSee U.S. price, payer contract price, or reimbursement rate was found; annual cost uses remote foot-monitoring and RPM analogs.
Company-stated FDA registration should not be interpreted as FDA approval, clearance, or authorization without confirmation in FDA device databases.
Commercial availability, EU registration status, U.S. claims, prescription requirements, and final payer billing pathway remain uncertain.

sources.title: Foot Temperature Measurement in People With Diabetes: Validation of a Non-Contact Thermal Device
supports: Technical report tested FeetSee InvCam against FlirA615 with FDA-approved TotalVision software as reference standard
Measurements were taken in 107 participants across active DFU, diabetes without ulcers, and healthy control groups
Reported strong agreement between devices with no systematic bias, intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.95, and typical error of 0.31 degrees
Authors concluded InvCam demonstrated validity for foot temperature measurement compared with the reference standard and is non-contact, reducing infection and cross-contamination risk

sources.title: 2023 IWGDF Prevention and Management of Diabetic Foot Disease Guideline Summary
supports: Guideline summary recommends considering coaching people with diabetes at moderate or high risk of foot ulceration to self-monitor foot skin temperatures once per day
Purpose is to identify early signs of foot inflammation and help prevent first or recurrent plantar foot ulcer

sources.title: Effectiveness of at-home skin temperature monitoring in reducing the incidence of foot ulcer recurrence in people with diabetes: a multicenter randomized controlled trial (DIATEMP)
supports: Randomized trial evaluated usual care plus daily plantar skin temperature monitoring in people with diabetes, neuropathy, and prior ulcer or Charcot neuro-arthropathy

Protocol used a temperature difference greater than 2.2 degrees C between corresponding left and right foot sites for two consecutive days to trigger reduced ambulatory activity and podiatrist contact
Primary-site recurrence was not significantly reduced in intention-to-treat analysis, but recurrence at any foot site was reduced and benefit depended on reducing ambulatory activity after hotspots
The trial highlights that temperature monitoring requires adherence and clinical action on hotspots to affect outcomes

sources.title: SmartMat+

Supports remote foot-temperature monitoring as an established device category for complex diabetes care

sources.title: Remote Patient Monitoring
supports: CMS describes RPM as patient-collected health data using a connected medical device that automatically transmits data to a health care provider
CMS states Medicare broadly covers RPM for physiologic data using a wide range of devices for chronic and acute conditions
Eligibility includes a chronic or acute condition requiring monitoring and a connected device that meets FDA's medical-device definition and digitally uploads data
CMS pays separately for education/setup, device supply, and treatment management components

sources.title: Remote Physiologic Monitoring (RPM)
supports: Aetna considers RPM medically necessary when the member has diabetes, heart failure, or hypertension requiring regular monitoring and management

Criteria include an FDA-approved or FDA-cleared device capable of automatic data transmission, use of data to inform treatment plan adjustment, qualified healthcare professional order/supervision, and documented consent
Aetna lists RPM CPT codes 99453, 99454, 99457, 99458, 99445, and 99470 when selection criteria are met
Aetna considers RPM experimental, investigational, or unproven when devices are not FDA approved or cleared

expected_launch_window.value: Not applicable to drug pipeline launch; device/diagnostic exclusion concern
expected_launch_window.method: Classified from ClinicalTrials.gov device/observational design, company device positioning, FDA registration language, and EU-funded market-preparation source rather than applying a drug launch forecast.
expected_launch_window.explanation: NCT07300163 is a device/diagnostic data-generation study, not a drug or pharma treatment pipeline asset. Company sources indicate FDA registration and EU market-preparation activity, but the assigned study does not establish a future drug launch event.

annual_cost_range.method: Used analog foot-temperature monitoring and RPM device-supply costs because no direct FeetSee price was found. Low equals Siren analog foot-monitoring subscription price of $19.95 per month x 12, rounded to $239. High equals RPM 99454 device supply rate $52.11 per month x 12 plus one-time 99453 setup/education estimate of $22, rounded to $647.
annual_cost_range.explanation: The range approximates device/service monitoring cost only and excludes direct FeetSee hardware pricing, clinician treatment-management time beyond device supply, payer discounts, care-management vendor fees, podiatry visits, wound care, and avoided-complication offsets.

clinical_differentiation.method: Weighted non-contact whole-foot thermal/optical imaging, app/cloud workflow, validation against reference thermography, and guideline support for temperature monitoring against the absence of prospective FeetSee outcome data and availability of analog mats/socks.
clinical_differentiation.explanation: FeetSee may improve usability for patients who have mobility, balance, contamination, or self-inspection barriers, but current differentiation remains modest until NCT07300163 or other prospective studies show reliable prediction and reduced DFU events.

budget_impact.method: Assessed analog annual device/service cost below $1,000, high-risk eligibility in prior DFU/peripheral neuropathy population, and likely medical-benefit/RPM controls rather than specialty-drug spend.
budget_impact.explanation: Per-patient cost is far below pharmaceutical specialty assets. Aggregate impact could rise with broad diabetes adoption, but appropriate targeting to prior DFU/high-risk neuropathy patients and RPM criteria should keep near-term pipeline budget impact low.

disruption_risk.method: Rated from observational/not-yet-recruiting status, device/diagnostic exclusion, no posted prospective outcome results, analog RPM coverage pathways, and low per-patient cost relative to drug pipeline assets.
disruption_risk.explanation: FeetSee may affect diabetic-foot monitoring workflows if validated and adopted, but it is unlikely to disrupt formulary operations or pharmacy pipeline planning because it is a device/diagnostic and not a treatment launch.

recommended_action.method: Mapped device/diagnostic exclusion concern, not-yet-recruiting observational study, no direct price, and existing RPM policy analogs to monitoring rather than active launch planning.
recommended_action.explanation: Track NCT07300163 recruitment/results, FDA database status, EU registration/market launch claims, pricing, and payer billing pathway. Do not treat this as a drug pipeline asset unless the dashboard includes device/diagnostic monitoring technologies.
